newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FORECAST-Australian jobs look for second rise.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Australian jobs look for second rise.

text.p: Australian employment is expected to show its second successive rise when May data is released on Thursday, but despite confidence of improving job prospects, analysts said the near term risks are for further weakness.

Such weakness would keep speculation about a fifth Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) rate cut bubbling, but would also raise questions over whether there was a need for something more than rate cuts to produce lower unemployment.
The median forecast of the 27 economists Reuters survyed was for a 15,000 rise in employment, with the unemployment rate remaining steady at 8.7 percent.

Reflecting the general confidence that employment has turned the corner and is gaining some strength, albeit slowly, only one economist of those surveyed was expecting negative jobs growth to follow on from the 37,100 rise posted in April.

However, while there are signs of strength in job vacancies and overtime data, economists said it was not yet assured that employment would recover strongly over the rest of 1997, which would keep markets looking for a rate cut.

"The risk in the numbers is that a weaker than expected May employment result -- flat or negative employment growth -- would heighten market speculation that another local rate cut may not be that far away," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
Employment growth, or more precisely a lack of it, has been a major factor behind the four interest rate cuts the RBA has delivered since last July.
Over the past year, employment has risen by just under 132,000 jobs -- an average of around 11,000 per month.

Of perhaps more concern than that sluggish headline growth figure has been the almost flat performance of fulltime employment. Over the past year, full-time employment has risen by only 13,100 -- at an average of just over 1,000 per month.
When announcing the latest cut on May 23, which took rates to 5.5 percent, the RBA said the economy was picking up from the second half of 1997, with employment seen strengthening.
While forward indicators suggested a firmer labour market ahead, economists said falls in unemployment would be slow, although stronger growth may see it moving towards eight percent by year-end.
One of the arguments that has arisen given the stubborn way the unemployment rate holds above 8.5 percent is whether there is a need for greater structural labour market reform.
"This is not just a code for lower wages, it is an attempt to make labour employable and productive, " Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen said.
"We will need to think long and hard about these issues over the next few years," he said.
RBA Governor Ian Macfarlane was another to have recently raised labour market reform as a means to lower unemployment.

Speaking in Melbourne on May 15, Macfarlane told his audience that "it seems reasonably apparent that while good economic growth is a very important part of reducing unemployment, growth alone will not be the answer."

The answer, as shown by lower unemployment rates in deregulated economies such as the U.S., Britain and New Zealand when compared to more regulated markets such as Western Europe and Australia, seemed to lie in further dergulation, he said.
However, these decisions were by their nature political, and Macfarlane said he did not want to go as far as the U.S. had in deregulation -- instead he sought a happy medium.
"All I am suggesting is that we should re-examine our labour market institutions to see whether they are protecting those in jobs at the expense of those looking for jobs," Macfarlane said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
